title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
claim: Investigates whether highly capable LLM agents require explicit self‑improvement directives, directly engaging the theme of language‑model agent loops and deterministic safety checks.

claim_verified.supporting_excerpt: An LLM agent is a loop: the model reasons about a goal, optionally calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats until done. Most of the interesting engineering isn't in the model — it's in what you let the agent touch, and where a human or a deterministic check sits before anything irreversible happens.

skeptic_objection: The excerpt discusses agent loops and safety checkpoints but never mentions or examines explicit self‑improvement directives, so the claim misreads the passage’s focus.

title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.
claim: Presents LMLineage for tracking content lineage and governing context across LLM agent sessions, aligning with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool standard theme.

claim_verified.supporting_excerpt: The Model Context Protocol standardizes how an application exposes tools and context to a model, so a tool built once can be reused across different agent frameworks instead of rewritten for each one.

skeptic_objection: The excerpt describes MCP as a standard for exposing reusable tools and context, not for tracking content lineage or governing context across sessions, so the claim mischaracterizes the protocol’s purpose.

title: Dynamic Task Allocation with Dialogue
abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires agents to adapt task allocation as goals and responsibilities evolve. Prior task-allocation frameworks often assume static goals, full observability, or rely on large language models (LLMs) without explicit, verifiable beliefs about task allocation or intent. These assumptions limit their applicability to real-world collaboration, where agents often lack full information about each other's actions, progress, or local environment. To support dynamic task allocation under partial observability, we introduce a communication-augmented Bayesian task-allocation framework. Our agent uses dialogue to reduce uncertainty about the environment and collaborators, while keeping decisions grounded in explicit probabilistic beliefs. We evaluate our framework in an Overcooked domain extended with dynamically arriving tasks under both full and partial object-space observability. Our communication agent consistently outperforms a vanilla LLM agent in both settings. Additionally, our framework performs comparably to a non-communicating task-allocation baseline under full observability, but substantially outperforms it under partial observability as task complexity increases by an average speed up of 0.585 and completes on average 18 timesteps faster. These results indicate that our agent is more efficient in dynamic task allocation than baselines in partially observable environments, and that communication is important as available information decreases.
claim: Proposes a dialogue‑driven dynamic task‑allocation framework for multi‑agent collaboration, addressing the multi‑agent systems coordination and error propagation theme.

claim_verified.supporting_excerpt: Multi-agent systems research explores how multiple LLM-driven agents coordinate to solve tasks no single agent handles well alone. Patterns worth tracking: hierarchical orchestration where a manager agent delegates to specialists, peer-to-peer negotiation, and shared-memory coordination. Open question: how do you stop one agent's error from silently propagating through the others?

skeptic_objection: The excerpt merely outlines coordination patterns and an open error‑propagation question, without actually proposing a dialogue‑driven dynamic task‑allocation framework.

title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.
claim: Introduces a tool‑calling strategy that stops exploration once sufficient information is gathered, linking to the tool use and interface contracts theme.

claim_verified.supporting_excerpt: Tool use lets an LLM extend its reasoning by calling external functions mid-generation. Key lesson: a tool's docstring is the interface contract — vague documentation causes far more wrong or missing arguments than the underlying model's raw capability would predict.

skeptic_objection: The excerpt never mentions a strategy for halting exploration once enough information is gathered, only the importance of clear docstrings as interface contracts.

title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.
claim: Develops a recursive self‑improvement architecture that balances fast System‑1 actions with deeper System‑2 reasoning, exemplifying language‑model agent loops and deterministic safety checks.

# Ecdysis: Efficient and Effective Training of Runtime Harnesses for LLM Agents

**arXiv ID**: 2609.11677v1

**Published Date**: 2026-09-10T15:09:08Z

**Authors**: Ruiqing Yue, Yu Cui, Zhuoyu Sun, Sicheng Pan, Xianhong Xue, Tingyu Li, Ting Li, Wenzhuo Zhu, Yi Chen, Yifei Liu, Baohan Huang, Zhe Cui, Haibin Zhang, Cong Zuo

**PDF**: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11677v1

## Abstract
Self-evolving runtime harnesses can substantially improve the capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents and provide a promising paradigm for optimizing agent execution. Existing harness evolution methods typically rely on iterative search, repeatedly evaluating and revising candidate harnesses based on execution feedback from task instances. While this paradigm enables continuous harness optimization, it incurs substantial time overhead due to repeated agent executions and code modifications, and may overfit to observed tasks and specific failure patterns, resulting in degraded generalization to unseen tasks. We identify the lack of principled failure diagnosis as a key bottleneck in harness evolution: an observed failure can reflect either model-specific deficiencies or systematic harness deficiencies, and directly optimizing against individual failures can lead to unnecessary model-specific accommodation. We therefore propose Ecdysis, an efficient and effective framework that distinguishes model-specific accommodation from harness-level repair and biases adaptation toward systematic harness deficiencies by identifying recurring cross-task failure patterns. Ecdysis adopts a batch-level cross-instance failure aggregation paradigm to jointly analyze failure evidence from multiple task instances and further introduces Failure-Driven Collaborative Refinement to diagnose failure causes and iteratively refine harness modification specifications. By combining cross-instance failure analysis with multi-role diagnosis, Ecdysis enables more effective harness evolution with lower training time. Experiments show that Ecdysis achieves up to a 1.84x speedup in harness training compared with existing harness evolution methods, while improving the reasoning accuracy of the resulting harnesses by 18.56%.

## Established Connection Claim
Describes Ecdysis, a method for training runtime harnesses that streamline LLM agent execution pipelines.

skeptic_objection: The excerpt never describes a recursive self‑improvement architecture or a System‑1/System‑2 dual‑process design, only a batch‑level failure‑driven method for training runtime harnesses.
